An episode has at most 15 turns and ends with an answer that starts with case closed , followed by a causal conclusion that cites the evidence, or case not closed , followed by what is established, what is missing, and a provisional assessment. The label of a report case is whether the official report determined the cause at the level its investigation pursued (the closure object in the reference); a report that establishes an event, such as a loss of engine power, but not its cause leaves the case open. Three tests. A single accuracy can be inflated either by the source of a case or by a conservative policy, so we evaluate closure with three tests, each closing one loophole: closure accuracy guards against recognising the source instead of reading the evidence; evidence dependence guards against closing out of habit, or stopping merely because evidence is scarce; and conclusion and gap quality guards against a right decision with a wrong or overstated conclusion. Closure accuracy. We report the rate of closing among cases that should close, the rate of not closing among cases that should not, and their mean (balanced accuracy), so that never closing is not rewarded. An answer without a closure marker counts as wrong on both sides. Every result is shown next to the source-only rule , which gives each source its majority training label. Within-source balanced accuracy computes balanced accuracy separately inside each report source and averages them; the source-only rule scores exactly 50 on it, so only reading the evidence can raise it. Evidence dependence. For cases labelled closed, we build a version without the items the conclusion rests on and a control without the same number of other items; the brief and question are unchanged, and removed items simply drop out of the index. The two versions differ only in whether the grounds are present, so the source is held fixed. We report the difference in closure rate between them (removed minus control; more negative means closure follows the evidence) and a two-class balanced accuracy per case, 1 2 ​ [ 𝟙 ​ ( control closed ) + 𝟙 ​ ( removed explicitly not closed ) ] \tfrac{1}{2}[\mathbb{1}(\text{control closed})+\mathbb{1}(\text{removed explicitly not closed})] . Conclusion and gap quality. A judge answers a fixed checklist about the final answer against the reference: whether the initiating cause is right, whether the causal chain matches, whether the answer overstates (presents as established what the evidence only suggests), what share of its causal claims cite evidence that was read and supports them, and whether it addresses alternative explanations. Our summary metric is the share of answers whose cause is right and not overstated. For unclosed answers the judge also checks whether the gap names specific evidence, whether that evidence is truly absent from the case, and whether it matches the reference’s reason for indeterminacy. The main judge is GPT-6 Sol; because it is also the teacher (§ 4 ), we repeat the checklist with Claude Sonnet 5 and Grok 4.7 (§ 6.3 , Appendix C ). 4 The Nautil Dataset Figure 2: Overview of Nautil. (1) Case files are built from four sources: evidence items with neutral titles are shown on demand, conclusions are withheld, and a hidden reference records whether the case should close; counterfactual versions and the OOD set follow the same format. (2) The teacher plans each investigation from the report and its label, a program assembles and checks it, Stage 2 adds citations and the hypothesis ledger, and audited trajectories train Nautil-SFT. (3) RLVR rewards only the closure decision, checked by a program. Right: one round of an actual Nautil-SFT investigation on a test case whose official finding is undetermined; after its checks weaken the fuel and engine explanations, it leaves the case open. Sources. Nautil draws on four kinds of investigation (Table 1 ). Boards : reports of four transport and chemical-safety boards (ATSB, RAIB, MAIB, CSB). NTSB : aviation final reports 2014–2024. NHTSA : vehicle defect investigations, with opening and closing summaries. Host : anomaly windows from a year of production server monitoring at a large internet company. Report cases take their label from whether the official report determined the cause. Host incidents have no report; their label is the teacher’s closure decision (below), which we use for training and report only in the appendix. Case files. For reports, an extraction pipeline (GPT-5.6 Sol) splits the text into factual, analytical and conclusion passages, turns factual passages into atomic evidence items with neutral titles, withholds any sentence that hints at the conclusion, writes the brief, anonymises identifiers, and records a hidden reference: whether the cause was determined, the official conclusion, rejected explanations and alternatives left open. E 1 E_{1} is fixed to the first four observation or measurement items of the primary source. For hosts, selected metric series are rendered as charts and described in text by a vision-language model that sees each chart with its numbers table and may quote only those numbers; a program flags any number not in the table. Service names are replaced by neutral roles, and addresses, alert IDs and dates are removed. Teacher trajectories. The teacher (GPT-6 Sol) sees the case file, the official analysis and the label, and plans an investigation: per turn, a note, the items to request and why, then a final answer (Stage 1). A program assembles the dialogue with tool returns copied verbatim, rejecting plans that cite unrequested items, contradict the label or leak withheld identifiers. Stage 2 adds exact citations and a ledger marking each hypothesis open, favoured or weakened, with every change citing visible evidence. For hosts the teacher also sees the closing report of a run of the JustDiag diagnostic harness ( Bi et al., 2026 ) on the incident. Trajectories are retraced from the report’s argument; their fetch order is not free exploration. Audit. The teacher scores each trajectory from − 5 -5 to + 5 +5 on alignment with the source, evidence grounding, active fetching, hypothesis updates and honest closure; we keep scores ≥ 4 \geq 4 without hard failures and allow one revision of the final answer for + 3 +3 . Of 1,345 generated report and host cases, 996 pass Stage 1, 818 pass Stage 2 and 518 (38.5%) pass the audit; with supplements for host not-closed cases, a salvage round and the removal of 26 cases whose brief and evidence came from different incidents, the final set has 731 cases. It is split 545 / 74 / 112 within each source, balancing labels and keeping each incident in one split. Table 1: Nautil by source. Items: median evidence items per case, over all cases of the source. Table 1 shows the structure that makes closure hard to measure: boards and hosts mostly close, NTSB and NHTSA mostly do not. Answering by source alone gives 83.0 balanced accuracy on the 64 non-host test cases (23 should close, 41 should not). This is why every closure result below is paired with the source-only rule and the within-source metric, and why the headline test set is non-host: host labels are teacher judgments, and the teacher itself, rerun under the same protocol, closes only 5 of the 39 host test cases labelled closed. Out-of-distribution test set. 141 cases from unseen domains: 83 reports (NTSB highway and pipeline, TSB Canada pipeline), 20 medical cases ( Wu et al., 2025 ) relabelled by whether the record contains the confirming finding, 18 microservice faults ( Pham et al., 2025 ) , and 20 Tennessee Eastman process runs ( Downs and Vogel, 1993 ; Rieth et al., 2017 ) . Domain and label are again tied, so we report the OOD set per domain and as a secondary column. Counterfactual versions. For the 62 test cases the teacher closes, the grounds are the items its final answer cites; versions remove 40%, 75% or 100% of them, and the control removes as many other items. A leak check flags removed items that may be restated elsewhere; 20 cases have none. 5 Training Nautil Investigators Supervised fine-tuning. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) (rank 16, α = 32 \alpha=32 , all linear layers) on the 545 training trajectories, with the native tool-call format, a 32k-token context, and loss on assistant turns only. We train two epochs (546 steps) and select the epoch-2 checkpoint before touching the test set: validation loss flattens after it, validation closure accuracy is highest, and its samples disagree most on the closure decision, which leaves room for RL. We call it Nautil-SFT. RLVR with a closure-only reward. Starting from Nautil-SFT, we run GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) in the same case environment. The reward is deliberately simple and fully checked by a program: r = D + s , D = { + 1 closure decision matches the label , − 1 it does not, or no closure marker , r=D+s,\qquad D=\begin{cases}+1&\text{closure decision matches the label},\\ -1&\text{it does not, or no closure marker},\end{cases} (1) where s ≤ 0 s\leq 0 is a format penalty (no citation in the final answer, citing unread or non-existent items, turns beyond six, repeated requests, malformed calls, a missing marker). Within each group, s s is centred separately among closing and non-closing rollouts, so that only D D separates the two decisions. No judge is called during training. Cases are drawn uniformly from the eight source × \times label strata, so that no source dominates the updates; host cases, whose labels are teacher judgments, make up a quarter of the draws. Each step samples 22 cases with 8 rollouts each (temperature 1.0, up to 15 turns); we use learning rate 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} , asymmetric clipping (0.2 / 0.28) ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , no KL term, and 50 steps on two H100 GPUs. We select step 30 as Nautil-RLVR with a screening evaluation that included 30 test cases (22 of them non-host); Appendix B reports results with those cases removed. We arrived at this reward after two judge-based variants performed worse (§ 6.4 ); full settings are in Appendix B . 6 Experiments Setup. All investigators run the same protocol, prompt and tool. We compare the untrained base model (Qwen3.5-9B), the base model prompted with ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) or with our note-and-ledger format, Abstain-R1 ( Zhai et al., 2026 ) and its 3B base model, Gemini 3.8 Flash as a frontier model, Nautil-SFT, Nautil-RLVR, and GPT-6 Sol as a teacher reference. 9B and 3B models are sampled three times per case; API models once, except Gemini on the non-host counterfactual cases (three times). Yes: training turns a model that closes almost everything into one that separates the two kinds of case, and not only by source (Table 2 ). The base model closes 81% of cases that should close but leaves only 18.7% of undetermined cases open, for 49.9 balanced accuracy. Nautil-SFT leaves 93.5% of undetermined cases open, the highest of all models, and reaches 69.2; Nautil-RLVR balances both sides (81.2 / 85.4) and reaches 83.3, on par with the teacher (81.8) and Gemini (79.3). Gemini reaches its score by closing every case that should close and 41% of those that should not. Within each source, where the source-only rule is at 50, Nautil-RLVR reaches 74.1 (Nautil-SFT 60.4, base 48.2), so its gains come from separating cases of the same source. Gemini’s 77.0 is helped by NHTSA and NTSB having only 2 and 3 should-close cases; on boards, the only source with enough cases on both sides, Nautil-RLVR reaches 78.7, Gemini 70.0 and Nautil-SFT 70.2 (differences within noise). Over the whole test set, Nautil-RLVR ties the source-only rule (83.3 vs. 83.0), which is why the next two tests matter. The Nautil-SFT numbers are unaffected by checkpoint selection; the Nautil-RLVR checkpoint was screened on a set that included 22 of the 64 test cases (Appendix B ). 6.2 Evidence dependence: do closures follow the evidence?
